pinnr

Physics-informed neural networks in native R.

pinnr trains neural networks that satisfy differential equations. Use it to solve ordinary and partial differential equations, or to estimate the unknown parameters of a model from observations. It runs on R’s torch, with no Python dependency, and it accepts ODE models written for deSolve without changes.

Why pinnr?

R has excellent classical solvers for differential equations, but physics-informed neural networks have so far required Python libraries such as DeepXDE, or R packages built for a single application. pinnr provides a general, R-native interface:

  • Use your deSolve models directly. pinn_ode() takes the same function(t, y, parms) you already wrote.
  • Estimate parameters from data. List unknown constants and supply observations; they are learned with the network. States can be partly observed, at different times, with missing values.
  • Write PDEs as R functions. Residuals are plain functions with arguments matched by name, and d(u, x, x) for derivatives.
  • Conditions for real problems. Dirichlet, Neumann, initial and custom (Robin, periodic, …) conditions, plus exact “hard” constraints through output transforms.
  • Practical training. Adam followed by optional L-BFGS, Latin hypercube sampling with resampling, time marching for long ODE horizons, GPU support, reproducible seeds, and stopping early with Esc without losing the model.

Installation

Install the pre-built package from R-universe:

install.packages("pinnr", repos = c("https://obasanmii.r-universe.dev",
                                    "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
torch::install_torch()   # once, if you have not used torch before

or the development version from GitHub:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("Obasanmii/pinnr")

On Intel Macs running macOS 14 or older, torch 0.17.0 cannot load its backend (its Intel build of LibTorch requires macOS 15). Install torch 0.16.3 instead, then run torch::install_torch().

Example: estimating epidemic parameters 

library(pinnr)

sir <- function(t, y, parms) {
  with(as.list(c(y, parms)), {
    dS <- -beta * S * I
    dI <- beta * S * I - gamma * I
    dR <- gamma * I
    list(c(dS, dI, dR))
  })
}
y0 <- c(S = 0.99, I = 0.01, R = 0)

# simulate observations of I and R with deSolve
ref <- as.data.frame(deSolve::ode(y0, 0:100, sir, c(beta = 0.3, gamma = 0.1)))
obs <- ref[ref$time %% 5 == 0, c("time", "I", "R")]

prob <- pinn_ode(sir, y0 = y0, times = 0:100,
                 unknown = c(beta = 0.5, gamma = 0.2), data = obs)
fit <- pinn_fit(prob, epochs = 5000, seed = 1)
coef(fit)
#>  beta gamma
#> ~0.30 ~0.10

Example: the heat equation 

heat <- pinn_problem(
  domain = pinn_domain(x = c(0, 1), t = c(0, 1)),
  outputs = "u",
  residual = function(u, x, t, a, d) d(u, t) - a * d(u, x, x),
  conditions = list(
    pinn_initial(function(x) sin(pi * x), time = "t"),
    pinn_dirichlet(where = list(x = "both"), value = 0)
  ),
  parms = list(a = 0.1)
)
fit <- pinn_fit(heat, epochs = 5000)
plot(fit, type = "solution")

See vignette("pinnr") or the website for a full walkthrough.

Main functions

Function Purpose
pinn_ode() Problem from a deSolve-style ODE model
pinn_problem(), pinn_domain() General PDE problem on a rectangular domain
pinn_dirichlet(), pinn_neumann(), pinn_initial(), pinn_condition() Conditions
pinn_fit() Train the network
predict(), residuals(), coef(), plot(), summary() Inspect a fit
pinn_save(), pinn_load() Store fits on disk

Limitations

pinnr is young. Domains are rectangles (time intervals, lines, boxes), residuals must use tensor-friendly operations, and, as with all PINNs, training is slower than a classical solver for problems those solvers handle well. PINNs are most useful for inverse problems, sparse or noisy data, and settings where a smooth, differentiable surrogate is helpful.

Contributing

Bug reports and pull requests are welcome; see CONTRIBUTING.md. Please open an issue to discuss larger changes first.

Citation

If you use pinnr in your work, please cite it; see citation("pinnr") or CITATION.cff. The method is from Raissi, Perdikaris and Karniadakis (2019), Journal of Computational Physics 378, 686-707, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcp.2018.10.045.
